html:
A wave of revolutions that swept across Europe in 1848, toppling or shaking governments in France, the German and Italian states, the Austrian Empire and beyond. Most were crushed within a year or two.

Bad harvests, hunger and an economic slump hit in 1846 and 1847. Liberals wanted constitutions and free speech, workers wanted jobs, and nationalists wanted their own states. In February, Paris rose and King Louis Philippe fled, and France became a republic again. The news set off risings in Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Venice, Budapest and Prague. Metternich, the symbol of the old order, fled Vienna. A parliament met in Frankfurt to draft a constitution for a united Germany.

The revolutionaries were divided, and armies stayed loyal to the kings. By 1849 Austria had retaken its cities, and Russian troops helped crush the Hungarian revolution. In France, Louis Napoleon was elected president and later made himself emperor.

Some changes lasted. Serfdom ended in the Austrian Empire, and Prussia kept a constitution. Many radicals emigrated, many to the United States. That February Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels had published the Communist Manifesto.
